explanation: SET NOCOUNT OFF leaves row-count messages enabled, adding unnecessary client and network chatter.
SET XACT_ABORT OFF lets some run-time errors leave open transactions only partially applied.
SELECT * from Sales.Orders couples callers to every current and future column.
SELECT TOP (10) o.OrderID from Sales.Orders has no ORDER BY, so the 10 rows are arbitrary.
DISTINCT on Sales.Orders.OrderID is redundant because OrderID is the primary key.
WITH (NOLOCK) on Sales.Orders can return uncommitted, missing, or duplicated rows.
YEAR(o.OrderDate) in the WHERE clause prevents a range seek on OrderDate.
The unlabelled year 2016 is embedded directly in the OrderDate filter.
int column o.CustomerID is compared to nvarchar variable @CustomerIdText, forcing a conversion.
@CustomerID IS NULL OR o.CustomerID = @CustomerID blocks a simple seek and harms cardinality estimates.
LIKE N'%urgent%' on o.Comments cannot use a normal index seek.
Business search term 'urgent' is embedded directly in the Comments predicate.
NOT IN (SELECT i.CustomerID ...) yields an empty result if the subquery produces NULL.
ISNULL(o.CustomerID, 0) = 1 wraps CustomerID and makes the predicate non-sargable.
CustomerID is compared to the hard-coded business value 1.
o.OrderID + 0 prevents direct index matching on OrderID.
o.CustomerID <> 1 is an inequality that typically scans a broad portion of Sales.Orders.
CustomerID is compared to the hard-coded business identifier 1.
CROSS JOIN of Sales.Orders and Sales.Customers has no join predicate and multiplies the rowsets.
SELECT TOP (1) from the Orders/Customers CROSS JOIN has no ORDER BY, so the row is arbitrary.
Comma join of Sales.Orders and Sales.OrderLines hides the join predicate in WHERE.
SELECT TOP (1) o.OrderID from the comma join has no ORDER BY, so the row is arbitrary.
Scalar COUNT(*) against Sales.OrderLines is executed once per Sales.Orders row.
Correlated EXISTS on Sales.OrderLines runs per outer order instead of a set join.
Quantity > 1 embeds a hard-coded business threshold in the EXISTS predicate.
The same CASE WHEN o.Comments IS NULL THEN 0 ELSE 1 END is repeated in the select list and ORDER BY.
ORDER BY 2 depends on select-list position and breaks if the column list changes.
OFFSET/FETCH ordered only by o.OrderDate has no unique tie-breaker, so pages can overlap or skip rows.
UNION removes duplicates between disjoint OrderID = 1 and OrderID = 2 branches that cannot overlap.
OrderID = 1 embeds a hard-coded business identifier.
OrderID = 2 embeds a second hard-coded business identifier.
COUNT(*) > 0 on Sales.OrderLines counts every matching line when only existence is required.
The COUNT(*) subquery is correlated on ol.OrderID = o.OrderID and runs per outer row.
SELECT @OrderID = o.OrderID from Sales.Orders silently keeps the last value if multiple rows qualify.
Table variable @OrderIds is likely to receive a poor cardinality estimate on older compatibility levels.
SELECT TOP (5) o.OrderID into @OrderIds has no ORDER BY, so which five orders are loaded is undefined.
SELECT ... INTO #ImplicitOrders creates the temp table schema implicitly instead of declaring it.
SELECT TOP (5) o.OrderID INTO #ImplicitOrders has no ORDER BY, so the loaded rows are arbitrary.
Cursor order_cursor walks Sales.Orders row by row instead of using a set-based operation.
The cursor source SELECT TOP (2) o.OrderID has no ORDER BY, so the two rows are arbitrary.
WHILE @Counter <= 1 performs iterative work that should be expressed as a set-based operation.
Dynamic SQL is built by concatenating CONVERT(nvarchar(20), @CustomerID) into the command text.
EXEC (@Sql) runs the concatenated string with no parameterized inputs.
Dynamic SQL is built by concatenating CONVERT(nvarchar(20), @OrderID) into the command text.
sys.sp_executesql @Sql is invoked without a parameter list, so the embedded value is not bound.
CREATE TABLE #Scratch is never dropped before the procedure ends.
CATCH only selects ERROR_MESSAGE() and neither rethrows nor returns a failure status.
RAISERROR is used for a new error path instead of THROW.
PRINT emits buffered diagnostic text instead of structured error or logging output.
o.CustomerID = 1 embeds a business identifier instead of using a parameter or lookup.
Unlabelled date constant '20160101' is embedded in the OrderDate filter.
date column o.OrderDate is compared to varchar literal '20160101', causing an implicit conversion.
CONVERT(date, '01/02/2016') has no style, so month and day can swap by session language.
Unlabelled date string '01/02/2016' is embedded in the conversion.
COALESCE on o.CustomerID and i.CustomerID in the join predicate blocks normal join optimization.
SELECT TOP (1) o.OrderID from the Orders/Invoices join has no ORDER BY, so the row is arbitrary.
Sales.Orders is self-joined on OrderID only to retrieve the same key already available on o.
SELECT TOP (1) o.OrderID from the self-join has no ORDER BY, so the row is arbitrary.
ORDER BY o.Comments sorts Sales.Orders by an unselective nvarchar(MAX) column.
SUM(ol.Quantity) aggregates the entire Sales.OrderLines fact table with no restrictive filter.
HAVING ol.OrderID > 0 applies a row-level predicate after grouping instead of filtering in WHERE.
ORDER BY OrderCount sorts a single-row COUNT(*) aggregate that has no GROUP BY.
COUNT(*) aggregates all of Sales.Orders with no restrictive filter.
MERGE on Sales.Orders has documented concurrency and correctness edge cases.
MERGE UPDATE SET target.Comments = target.Comments writes the current value and still logs and locks.
UPDATE Sales.Orders SET Comments = Comments changes no data but still causes logging and locking.
DELETE FROM Sales.OrderLines WHERE Quantity = -1 uses a broad non-key predicate and can remove many rows.
Quantity = -1 embeds a hard-coded business value in the DELETE predicate.
WAITFOR DELAY '00:00:01' blocks a worker instead of using asynchronous scheduling.
BEGIN TRANSACTION is started outside a TRY/CATCH, so errors can leave the transaction open.
SET IDENTITY_INSERT Sales.Orders ON changes session state and couples the procedure to identity management.
EXEC sp_who calls a system routine without a schema qualifier.
SET ROWCOUNT 1 changes a session setting and is never restored to 0.
INSERT INTO #DemoCategories VALUES (...) omits an explicit column list.
CategoryID value 99 is a hard-coded business identifier in the INSERT.
INSERT INTO #DemoCustomers SELECT ... omits an explicit column list.
CustomerName LIKE '%' + @CustomerName + '%' starts with a wildcard and cannot seek on the unique name index.
Dynamic SQL concatenates @CustomerName directly into the LIKE pattern string.
User-supplied @CustomerName is concatenated into executable SQL and can inject arbitrary commands.
The dynamic LIKE ''%... pattern begins with a wildcard and cannot seek on CustomerName.
sp_executesql @sql is executed without binding @CustomerName as a parameter.
EXEC sp_executesql is called without a schema qualifier.
UPDATE #DemoCustomers SET CustomerCategoryID = 1 has no WHERE clause and updates every row.
CustomerCategoryID is set to the hard-coded business identifier 1.
WHERE o.OrderDate >= '2016-01-01' on the LEFT JOINed Sales.Orders table converts the join to an inner join.
Unlabelled date constant '2016-01-01' is embedded in the OrderDate filter.
date column o.OrderDate is compared to varchar literal '2016-01-01', causing an implicit conversion.
Date string '2016-01-01' is converted without an explicit style parameter.
DeliveryMethodID = NULL is UNKNOWN for every row; use IS NULL instead.
Scalar UDF dbo.GetCustomerType(CustomerID) in the SELECT list forces row-by-row evaluation.
CATCH only selects ERROR_MESSAGE() and neither rethrows nor returns a failure status.
CATCH after BEGIN TRANSACTION does not ROLLBACK, leaving the transaction open when XACT_ABORT is OFF.
WITH (INDEX = 1) on Sales.Customers hard-codes an index hint in production code.
Three nested derived tables around Sales.Customers should be refactored to a CTE or temp table.
CustomerName LIKE '%A%' starts with a wildcard and cannot seek on the unique name index.
LIKE pattern '%A%' embeds a hard-coded search value.
SELECT * from dbo.GetCustomerOrdersMulti couples callers to every column the function returns.
dbo.GetCustomerOrdersMulti is used as a multi-statement TVF where an inline TVF would optimize better.
